title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text: A volcano plot is the workhorse of differential-expression analysis: log fold change on x, statistical significance on y, and the interesting genes pushed out to the top corners. In this post we build one in R with canvasXpress — interactive (zoom, hover, filter), and, importantly, reproducible: the whole figure is a single portable specification you can store, validate and re-render from R, Python or JavaScript.

title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
Install

install.packages("canvasXpress")

title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
A differential-expression table
For a self-contained example we simulate 1,000 genes. Swap this block for your own results table (e.g. the output of limma::topTable() or DESeq2::results()) — you need a log fold change and a significance value per gene.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
n     <- 1000
genes <- paste0("Gene", seq_len(n))

# Simulate a realistic volcano: most genes have no real effect, a minority are
# differentially expressed. Significance follows effect size / standard error, which
# is what gives a volcano its shape.
de     <- runif(n) < 0.12                                   # ~12% truly changed
sgn    <- sample(c(-1, 1), n, replace = TRUE)
effect <- ifelse(de, sgn * (0.8 + 0.9 * runif(n)), 0)       # true log2FC
se     <- 0.22 + 0.5 * runif(n)                             # per-gene standard error
logFC  <- round(effect + rnorm(n, 0, se), 3)               # observed log2FC
pval   <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(logFC / se))                       # z-test p-value
negLogP <- round(pmin(-log10(pval), 16), 3)

# Classify each gene by effect size + significance
group <- ifelse(logFC >  1 & negLogP > 1.3, "Increased",
         ifelse(logFC < -1 & negLogP > 1.3, "Decreased", "NoChange"))

canvasXpress expects a numeric matrix/data frame of values (genes in rows) plus an optional variable annotation table carrying per-gene attributes — here the regulation call and the fold change we’ll use for point size.

y <- data.frame(
  "logFC"     = logFC,
  "-log-pVal" = negLogP,
  row.names   = genes,
  check.names = FALSE
)

varAnnot <- data.frame(
  Group = group,
  FC    = round(2^abs(logFC), 2),
  row.names   = genes,
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
The plot

canvasXpress(
  data     = y,
  varAnnot = varAnnot,
  graphType = "Scatter2D",
  xAxis    = list("logFC"),
  yAxis    = list("-log-pVal"),
  colorBy  = "Group",
  colorKey = list(Group = list(
    Increased = "rgba(197,27,38,0.75)",
    Decreased = "rgba(33,102,172,0.75)",
    NoChange  = "rgba(150,150,150,0.35)"
  )),
  sizeBy   = "FC",
  sizes    = c(3, 6, 9, 12, 15),
  title    = "Publication-ready volcano plot",
  xAxisTitle = "log2 fold change",
  yAxisTitle = "-log10 p-value",
  showDecorations = TRUE,
  decorations = list(line = list(
    list(color = "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", width = 1, x =  1),
    list(color = "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", width = 1, x = -1),
    list(color = "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", width = 1, y = 1.301)
  )),
  width  = 650,
  height = 500
)





The chart is interactive: hover a point for its gene and values, drag to zoom, or use the toolbar to filter by regulation group. The dashed guides mark the ±1 log2FC and the p = 0.05 cutoffs.

title: Interactive volcano plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
Why “reproducible”
Everything above serializes to one JSON specification — the data and the config. That spec is portable: the identical figure renders from the Python (canvasxpress) and JavaScript packages, and it can be validated against a published schema and re-rendered later, so a figure in a paper can be regenerated and audited rather than just looked at.

title: Violin and half (split) violin plots in R with canvasXpress
text: A violin plot shows the full shape of a distribution — where the density is thick or thin — instead of collapsing it to a box’s quartiles. And when you want to compare two conditions at the same position, a split (half) violin puts one condition on each half. Here we build both in R with canvasXpress: interactive, and reproducible because the figure is one portable spec.

title: Violin and half (split) violin plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
The data
A measurement across a few dose groups and two conditions. Swap in your own long-format table.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
doses <- c("Low", "Medium", "High"); conds <- c("Control", "Treated")
value <- c(); Dose <- c(); Condition <- c()
for (d in doses) for (co in conds) {
  mu <- if (d == "Low") 6 else if (d == "Medium") 8 else 10
  if (co == "Treated") mu <- mu + 1.5
  value <- c(value, round(rnorm(40, mu, 1.2), 2))
  Dose <- c(Dose, rep(d, 40)); Condition <- c(Condition, rep(co, 40))
}

In canvasXpress terms a violin is a Boxplot graph with the violin turned on: one measured variable × N observations, with the grouping columns as smpAnnot.

ids <- paste0("o", seq_along(value))
y <- data.frame(matrix(value, nrow = 1, dimnames = list("value", ids)), check.names = FALSE)
smpAnnot <- data.frame(Dose = Dose, Condition = Condition, row.names = ids, check.names = FALSE)

title: Violin and half (split) violin plots in R with canvasXpress
text:
A full violin per group
showViolinBoxplot = TRUE draws the violin (with a small boxplot inside); violinScale = "area" makes equal-area violins.

canvasXpress(
  data = y, smpAnnot = smpAnnot, graphType = "Boxplot",
  showViolinBoxplot = TRUE, violinScale = "area",
  groupingFactors = list("Dose"), xAxis = list("value"),
  smpTitle = "Dose", title = "Distribution of value by dose",
  width = 650, height = 500
)

title: Violin and half (split) violin plots in R with canvasXpress
section: A split (half) violin comparing two conditions
text:
A split (half) violin comparing two conditions
Group by both factors, colour by the condition, and set violinSide = "split" — the two conditions share each dose position, one on each half. This reads far better than two full violins side by side.

canvasXpress(
  data = y, smpAnnot = smpAnnot, graphType = "Boxplot",
  showViolinBoxplot = TRUE, violinScale = "area",
  groupingFactors = list("Dose", "Condition"), colorBy = "Condition",
  violinSide = "split", violinTrim = FALSE, xAxis = list("value"),
  smpTitle = "Dose", title = "Control vs Treated — split violin by dose",
  width = 650, height = 500
)





Hover to read the density and summary stats. violinSide can also be "lt" or "rb" for a one-sided half violin (handy for a raincloud when paired with violinPointsSide).

title: Genome browser tracks in R with canvasXpress
text: A genome browser view stacks tracks that share one coordinate axis: coverage, gene models, variants. In R this usually means Gviz or ggbio. Here we build an interactive, zoomable view with canvasXpress — and the whole thing is one portable spec.

title: Genome browser tracks in R with canvasXpress
text:
The data shape
A Genome figure is a list of tracks that share one coordinate axis — each with a type. Real browser views stack several: here we build four — gene models (box, multi-exon, connected), coverage across three tissues (bar), an expression heatmap (heatmap), and variant markers (triangle).

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(3)

# Gene models: each gene is a set of exon [start, end] intervals, drawn connected.
genes <- lapply(0:3, function(j) {
  start <- 40 + j * 120
  exons <- lapply(0:(sample(2:4, 1) - 1), function(k) list(start + k * 30, start + k * 30 + 18))
  list(id = paste0("GENE", j + 1), dir = if (j %% 2 == 0) "right" else "left",
       fill = "rgb(70,130,220)", outline = "rgb(0,0,0)", data = exons)
})

# Coverage and expression: one entry per binned position, three tissues each.
offsets  <- 50 + (0:21) * 22
coverage <- lapply(seq_along(offsets), function(i)
  list(id = paste0("p", i), offset = offsets[i],
       data = list(sample(8:45, 1), sample(8:45, 1), sample(8:45, 1))))
express  <- lapply(seq_along(offsets), function(i)
  list(id = paste0("p", i), offset = offsets[i],
       data = list(round(rnorm(1), 2), round(rnorm(1), 2), round(rnorm(1), 2))))

# Variants: point markers at genomic positions.
snps <- lapply(0:8, function(k)
  list(id = paste0("rs", 1000 + k), offset = sample(45:520, 1),
       fill = "rgb(200,40,40)", outline = "rgb(0,0,0)"))

genome <- list(tracks = list(
  list(name = "Genes (exon models)", type = "box", connect = TRUE, data = genes),
  list(name = "Coverage — Heart / Liver / Kidney", type = "bar", height = 120,
       fill = "rgb(80,80,200)", outline = "rgb(60,60,60)", data = coverage),
  list(name = "Expression (z-score)", type = "heatmap", height = 90, data = express),
  list(name = "SNPs", type = "triangle", data = snps)
))

title: Genome browser tracks in R with canvasXpress
text:
The plot
The Genome graph type is passed through to the engine as-is; featureStaggered spreads crowded features so labels stay legible.

canvasXpress(
  data            = genome,
  graphType       = "Genome",
  background       = "rgb(245,245,245)",
  featureStaggered = TRUE,
  title            = "Multi-track genome browser: genes, coverage, expression and variants",
  width            = 760,
  height           = 520
)

The Genome graphType is an advanced chart, data is passed as-is to the JS library






Scroll/drag to pan and zoom into a region; every track stays locked to the shared coordinate axis, so the gene models, coverage, expression and variants line up position-for-position. Swap each track for your own pileup, annotation and VCF-derived data.

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in R with canvasXpress
text: Kaplan–Meier curves summarize time-to-event data: the step-down survival probability over time, usually split by a group like treatment arm. In this post we build one in R with canvasXpress. canvasXpress computes the survival steps for you — you hand it a time column and a censoring column, and it does the rest — and the result is an interactive figure that serializes to one portable, reproducible spec.

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in R with canvasXpress
text:
A survival table
Swap this simulated block for your own data: you need, per subject, a follow-up time, a censoring indicator (1 = censored, 0 = event), and the grouping variable.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
n    <- 200
arm  <- sample(c("Treatment", "Control"), n, replace = TRUE)
base <- ifelse(arm == "Treatment", 60, 40)      # treatment survives longer
time <- round(rexp(n, rate = 1 / base), 1)
cens <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)                        # 1 = censored, 0 = event
subj <- paste0("Subj", seq_len(n))

canvasXpress reads two columns for a Kaplan–Meier plot — the time and its matching censor flag — plus a per-subject annotation carrying the group.

y <- data.frame(
  "Time"        = time,
  "Time-Censor" = cens,
  row.names     = subj,
  check.names   = FALSE
)

varAnnot <- data.frame(Arm = arm, row.names = subj, check.names = FALSE)

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in R with canvasXpress
text:
The plot
The key is graphType = "KaplanMeier" and passing both columns to xAxis (time first, then the censor column). colorBy stratifies the curves.

canvasXpress(
  data     = y,
  varAnnot = varAnnot,
  graphType = "KaplanMeier",
  xAxis    = list("Time", "Time-Censor"),
  colorBy  = "Arm",

The data shape
A Genome figure is a list of tracks that share one coordinate axis — each with a type. Real browser views stack several: here we build four — gene models (box, multi-exon, connected), coverage across three tissues (bar), an expression heatmap (heatmap), and variant markers (triangle).

import random
random.seed(3)

# Gene models: each gene is a set of exon [start, end] intervals, drawn connected.
genes = []
for j in range(4):
    start = 40 + j * 120
    exons = [[start + k * 30, start + k * 30 + 18] for k in range(random.randint(2, 4))]
    genes.append({"id": f"GENE{j+1}", "dir": "right" if j % 2 == 0 else "left",
                  "fill": "rgb(70,130,220)", "outline": "rgb(0,0,0)", "data": exons})

# Coverage and expression: one entry per binned position, three tissues each.
offsets  = [50 + i * 22 for i in range(22)]
coverage = [{"id": f"p{i}", "offset": o,
             "data": [random.randint(8, 45), random.randint(8, 45), random.randint(8, 45)]}
            for i, o in enumerate(offsets)]
express  = [{"id": f"p{i}", "offset": o,
             "data": [round(random.gauss(0, 1), 2) for _ in range(3)]}
            for i, o in enumerate(offsets)]

# Variants: point markers at genomic positions.
snps = [{"id": f"rs{1000+k}", "offset": random.randint(45, 520),
         "fill": "rgb(200,40,40)", "outline": "rgb(0,0,0)"} for k in range(9)]

data = {"tracks": [
    {"name": "Genes (exon models)", "type": "box", "connect": True, "data": genes},
    {"name": "Coverage — Heart / Liver / Kidney", "type": "bar", "height": 120,
     "fill": "rgb(80,80,200)", "outline": "rgb(60,60,60)", "data": coverage},
    {"name": "Expression (z-score)", "type": "heatmap", "height": 90, "data": express},
    {"name": "SNPs", "type": "triangle", "data": snps},
]}

text:
The data shape
canvasXpress builds a network from two lists: nodes (id, name, group) and edges (id1, id2, value). Swap this simulated three-community graph for your own.

import random
random.seed(1)

groups = ["Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma"]
nodes, by_group = [], {g: [] for g in groups}
k = 0
for g in groups:
    for i in range(7):
        nid = f"n{k}"; nodes.append({"id": nid, "name": f"{g}{i+1}", "group": g})
        by_group[g].append(nid); k += 1

edges = []
for g in groups:                                   # dense within a community
    m = by_group[g]
    for i in range(len(m)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(m)):
            if random.random() < 0.5:
                edges.append({"id1": m[i], "id2": m[j], "value": random.randint(1, 5)})
for _ in range(6):                                 # a few cross-community links
    g1, g2 = random.sample(groups, 2)
    edges.append({"id1": random.choice(by_group[g1]), "id2": random.choice(by_group[g2]), "value": 1})

title: Sankey / alluvial diagrams in Python with canvasxpress
text: A Sankey (or alluvial) diagram shows how a quantity flows through a sequence of categorical stages — patients moving from a cohort, to a treatment, to an outcome; or reads from a sample, to a mapping status, to a feature. The width of each stream is the magnitude. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — interactive and reproducible.

title: Sankey / alluvial diagrams in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Install
pip install canvasxpress

title: Sankey / alluvial diagrams in Python with canvasxpress
text:
The data shape
canvasXpress builds a Sankey from a table where each row is one path through the stages, plus a frequency/weight. Swap this simulated clinical flow for your own counts.

import random
random.seed(1)

cohorts  = ["Cohort A", "Cohort B"]
treats   = ["Drug 1", "Drug 2", "Placebo"]
outcomes = ["Response", "Stable", "Progression"]

Cohort, Treatment, Outcome, Freq = [], [], [], []
for co in cohorts:
    for tr in treats:
        for ou in outcomes:
            base = 40 if ou == "Response" else 25 if ou == "Stable" else 15
            if tr == "Placebo" and ou == "Response":
                base = 12                                   # placebo responds less
            Cohort.append(co); Treatment.append(tr); Outcome.append(ou)
            Freq.append(base + random.randint(0, 15))

The value (Freq) is the single measured variable; the stage columns are sample annotations (x).

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

ids = [f"r{i+1}" for i in range(len(Freq))]
data = {
    "y": {"vars": ["Freq"], "smps": ids, "data": [Freq]},
    "x": {"Cohort": Cohort, "Treatment": Treatment, "Outcome": Outcome},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Sankey",
    "sankeyAxes": ["Cohort", "Treatment", "Outcome"],
    "xAxis": ["Freq"],
    "colorBy": "Outcome",
    "sankeyType": "proportional",
    "graphOrientation": "horizontal",
    "title": "Patient flow: cohort to treatment to outcome",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="sankey", data=data, config=config, width=700, height=500)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)






  






Hover any stream to see the count; the widths are proportional to the frequency, so you can read the flow at a glance. sankeyType can also be "aligned" (classic alluvial) or "equal".

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
text: Kaplan–Meier curves summarize time-to-event data: the step-down survival probability over time, usually split by a group like treatment arm. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — it computes the survival steps for you from a time column and a censoring column — and the result is interactive and reproducible.

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Install
pip install canvasxpress

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
text:
A survival table
Swap this simulated block for your own data: per subject you need a follow-up time, a censoring indicator (1 = censored, 0 = event), and the grouping variable.

import numpy as np

rng  = np.random.default_rng(1)
n    = 200
arm  = rng.choice(["Treatment", "Control"], n)
base = np.where(arm == "Treatment", 60, 40)     # treatment survives longer
time = np.round(rng.exponential(base), 1)
cens = rng.binomial(1, 0.3, n)                  # 1 = censored, 0 = event
subj = [f"Subj{i+1}" for i in range(n)]

title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Build the spec
The two columns — the time and its matching censor flag — go in as the variable samples, and the arm rides along as a variable annotation. The key is graphType="KaplanMeier" and passing both columns to xAxis.

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    # Subjects are the variables (rows); each row holds [Time, Time-Censor].
    "y": {"vars": subj, "smps": ["Time", "Time-Censor"],
          "data": [[t, c] for t, c in zip(time.tolist(), cens.tolist())]},
    "z": {"Arm": arm.tolist()},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "KaplanMeier",
    "xAxis": ["Time", "Time-Censor"],
    "colorBy": "Arm",
    "title": "Overall survival by treatment arm",
    "xAxisTitle": "Time (weeks)", "yAxisTitle": "Probability of survival",
    "invertCensored": True,               # draw censoring ticks
    "showKMConfidenceIntervals": False,
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="km", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=500)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)

title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
text: A volcano plot is the workhorse of differential-expression analysis: log fold change on x, statistical significance on y, and the interesting genes pushed to the top corners. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — interactive (zoom, hover, filter) and reproducible: the whole figure is one portable specification you can store and re-render from Python, R or JavaScript.

title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Install
pip install canvasxpress

title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
text:
A differential-expression table
Swap this simulated block for your own results — the output of any DE pipeline works, as long as you have a log fold change and a significance value per gene.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import norm

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 1000
genes = [f"Gene{i+1}" for i in range(n)]

# Simulate a realistic volcano: most genes have no real effect, a minority are
# differentially expressed. Significance follows effect size / standard error, which
# is what gives a volcano its shape.
de     = rng.random(n) < 0.12                              # ~12% truly changed
sign   = rng.choice([-1, 1], n)
effect = np.where(de, sign * (0.8 + 0.9 * rng.random(n)), 0.0)   # true log2FC
se     = 0.22 + 0.5 * rng.random(n)                        # per-gene standard error
logfc  = effect + rng.normal(0, se)                        # observed log2FC
pval   = 2 * norm.sf(np.abs(logfc / se))                   # z-test p-value
neglogp = np.minimum(-np.log10(pval), 16)

df = pd.DataFrame({"logFC": logfc.round(3), "-log-pVal": neglogp.round(3)}, index=genes)

def classify(fc, p):
    if fc > 1 and p > 1.3:   return "Increased"
    if fc < -1 and p > 1.3:  return "Decreased"
    return "NoChange"

group = [classify(fc, p) for fc, p in zip(df["logFC"], df["-log-pVal"])]
fold  = (2 ** df["logFC"].abs()).round(2)

title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Build the spec
canvasxpress takes a data object (a value matrix plus annotations) and a config. We put the two measurements as the variable’s samples and carry the regulation call and fold change as variable annotations (z).

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    # Genes are the variables (rows); each row holds [logFC, -log-pVal].
    "y": {"vars": genes, "smps": ["logFC", "-log-pVal"],
          "data": [[fc, p] for fc, p in zip(df["logFC"], df["-log-pVal"])]},
    "z": {"Group": group, "FC": fold.tolist()},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Scatter2D",
    "title": "Publication-ready volcano plot",
    "xAxis": ["logFC"], "yAxis": ["-log-pVal"],
    "xAxisTitle": "log2 fold change", "yAxisTitle": "-log10 p-value",
    "colorBy": "Group",
    "colorKey": {"Group": {"Increased": "rgba(197,27,38,0.75)",
                            "Decreased": "rgba(33,102,172,0.75)",
                            "NoChange":  "rgba(150,150,150,0.35)"}},
    "sizeBy": "FC", "sizes": [3, 6, 9, 12, 15],
    "showDecorations": True,
    "decorations": {"line": [
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "x": 1},
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "x": -1},
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "y": 1.301},
    ]},
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="volcano", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=500)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)






  






The chart is interactive — hover a point for its gene and values, drag to zoom, filter by regulation group in the toolbar. The dashed guides mark the ±1 log2FC and p = 0.05 cutoffs.

title: Choropleth maps in Python with canvasxpress
text: A choropleth shades each region by a value — emissions, incidence, turnout, income. It is the most common map in data analysis and the easiest to get subtly wrong: most “my map is all one colour” complaints are not rendering bugs but scale bugs. Here we build a choropleth in Python with canvasxpress that stays vivid and honest on exactly the kind of heavy-tailed data that flattens naive maps. The join and the colouring happen inside the render, so every figure is one portable spec you can re-run from Python, R or the browser.

title: Choropleth maps in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Install
pip install canvasxpress pandas

title: Choropleth maps in Python with canvasxpress
section: First, the trap: colour encodes a rate, not a count
text:
First, the trap: colour encodes a rate, not a count
A choropleth fills an area, and area is a size channel your eye cannot help reading. Shade regions by a raw count — total cases, total emissions, total sales — and big, populous regions light up simply because they are big and populous. You have drawn a population map with extra steps.
The fix is almost always to map a rate or density: cases per 100k, emissions per capita, sales per store. Reserve raw counts for a proportional-symbol map (a sized bubble at each centroid), where the size channel carries the count honestly. Decide which question you are answering before you pick the geometry — this one choice prevents most misleading maps.

title: Choropleth maps in Python with canvasxpress
text:
One value per region
A choropleth needs exactly one measurement per shape. In canvasxpress the columns (smps) are the regions — they match the map by name — and each row (vars) is a variable you can colour by. Here it’s CO₂ emissions per country for 2018. We load a prepared table; swap it for your own (any country → value table works).

import pandas as pd

dat = pd.read_csv(
    "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-dat.txt",
    sep="\t", index_col=0,
)
smp = pd.read_csv(
    "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-smp.txt",
    sep="\t", index_col=0,
).reindex(dat.columns)        # align annotation to the country order

print(dat.shape)              # (1, N): one row (CO2) x N countries

title: Choropleth maps in Python with canvasxpress
section: The map: quantile classes on a viridis ramp
text:
The map: quantile classes on a viridis ramp
y carries the matrix (vars = the variable, smps = the countries, data = the values); the optional x block adds per-country annotations (continent, ISO code) for richer tooltips. The two choices that make this map work are in the colour scale: a seven-stop viridis colorSpectrum, and colorSpectrumBreaksMethod = "quantile", which puts an equal number of countries in every colour class. On skewed data that guarantee is what keeps all seven colours on the map.

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    "y": {
        "vars": list(dat.index),            # ["CO2"]
        "smps": list(dat.columns),          # country names
        "data": dat.values.tolist(),        # [[values]]
    },
    "x": {
        "Continent": smp["Continent"].tolist(),
        "Code":      smp["Code"].tolist(),
    },
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Map",
    "colorBy":   "CO2",
    "topoJSON":  "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
    "mapId":     "co2Quantile",
    "colorSpectrum": ["#440154", "#443983", "#31688e", "#21918c",
                      "#35b779", "#90d743", "#fde725"],
    "colorSpectrumBreaksMethod": "quantile",
    "mapColor":        "#d9dde3",
    "mapOutlineColor": "#ffffff",
    "legendPosition":  "bottom",
    "title":    "CO2 emissions per country (2018)",
    "subtitle": "Seven quantile classes: each colour holds about 28 of 198 countries",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="co2quant", data=data, config=config, width=760, height=520)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)






  






Every band of the ramp is doing work: the darkest purples are the smallest emitters, the yellows the largest, and the legend’s break values tell you the class edges are data-driven, not evenly spaced. Hover any country for its name, continent and value.

title: Choropleth maps in Python with canvasxpress
section: Why not just a plain linear ramp?
text:
Why not just a plain linear ramp?
Because the data is heavy-tailed — a few countries emit thousands of megatonnes while most emit almost nothing. On a linear scale, 195 of these 198 countries fall into the bottom fifth of the range, so a continuous ramp paints nearly the whole world one pale tone and spends its colour on two or three outliers:

linear = {
    "graphType": "Map",
    "colorBy":   "CO2",
    "topoJSON":  "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
    "mapId":     "co2Linear",
    "legendPosition": "left",
    "theme": "solarized",
    "title":    "The same data on a plain linear ramp",
    "subtitle": "195 of 198 countries sit in the bottom fifth of the scale - the map goes flat",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="co2lin", data=data, config=linear, width=700, height=480)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)






  






This is the single most common choropleth failure. The cure is classing:

"colorSpectrumBreaksMethod": "quantile" — equal counts per class. Every colour is used, by construction. The right default for skewed data and for “which regions rank high/low” questions.
"colorSpectrumBreaksMethod": "jenks" — natural breaks that minimise within-class variance. Best when the data has genuine clusters with gaps between them; on smoothly heavy-tailed data like this it piles almost everything into the bottom class, so check the legend before you trust it.
Three to seven classes is the usable range — beyond that, readers cannot match colours to the legend.

title: Choropleth maps in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Choose the palette on purpose
The palette is the scale’s grammar, not decoration:

Sequential (dark → light of ordered hues, like viridis above) for a quantity that only goes up: counts, rates, concentrations.
Diverging (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint) when values are meaningful above and below a reference: change vs. last year, difference from a target, a signed index. Give a three-colour colorSpectrum and pin the midpoint with colorSpectrumZeroValue:
"colorBy": "Change",
"colorSpectrum": ["#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"],  # blue - neutral - red
"colorSpectrumZeroValue": 0,                          # value mapped to the middle colour
Never use a diverging palette for a purely positive quantity — the neutral midpoint invents a “normal” the data does not have.

Viridis and the ColorBrewer ramps are colour-blind-safe and perceptually ordered; a rainbow ramp is neither, so readers cannot tell which end means “more”. Keep the same scale across small multiples so maps stay comparable.

title: Choropleth maps in Python with canvasxpress
section: Polish: legend, labels and base styling
text:
Polish: legend, labels and base styling

subtitle / source — caption units and provenance.
"legendNumberFormat": {"style": "decimal", "decimals": 1, "suffix": "%"} — format legend ticks.
mapColor / mapOutlineColor — the fill for no-data regions (a neutral grey) and the shape borders, so missing data reads as missing rather than as a value.
"showMapLabels": True — draw region names (best on few-region maps; clutters a world map).
"legendInside": True — float the legend over empty ocean to reclaim width.

title: Choropleth maps in Python with canvasxpress
text:
Beyond the world map

Other boundaries. Point topoJSON at any shape file — US states, a country’s provinces, counties, custom districts. The join key is just the shape name.
Projection. "mapProjection": "albers" (equal-area) or "mercator". Equal-area projections matter for choropleths: Mercator inflates high latitudes and exaggerates their visual weight.
Categorical maps. Point colorBy at a categorical column for a qualitative choropleth with a discrete legend.
Markers. Add decorations to drop labelled points on cities or call out specific regions.

The whole figure — data, boundaries, classing rule and palette — is one portable spec you can store, validate and re-render from R or JavaScript.

title: Interactive network graphs in R with canvasXpress
text: A network graph shows relationships: nodes connected by edges, laid out so that connected things sit near each other. The usual R reach is igraph or networkD3, but here we build one with canvasXpress — draggable, hover-labelled, force-directed, and reproducible, because the whole figure is one portable data + config spec.

title: Interactive network graphs in R with canvasXpress
text:
The data shape
canvasXpress builds a network from two tables: nodes (id, name, group) and edges (id1, id2, value). Swap this simulated three-community graph for your own.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
grp   <- rep(c("Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma"), each = 7)
ids   <- paste0("n", seq_along(grp))
nodes <- data.frame(id = ids, name = paste0(grp, ave(grp, grp, FUN = seq_along)),
                    group = grp, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Dense within a community, sparse between communities — the structure a layout reveals.
e1 <- c(); e2 <- c(); ev <- c()
for (g in unique(grp)) {
  m <- ids[grp == g]
  for (i in seq_along(m)) for (j in seq_along(m))
    if (i < j && runif(1) < 0.5) { e1 <- c(e1, m[i]); e2 <- c(e2, m[j]); ev <- c(ev, sample(1:5, 1)) }
}
for (k in 1:6) {                                     # a few cross-community links
  pair <- sample(unique(grp), 2)
  e1 <- c(e1, sample(ids[grp == pair[1]], 1)); e2 <- c(e2, sample(ids[grp == pair[2]], 1)); ev <- c(ev, 1)
}
edges <- data.frame(id1 = e1, id2 = e2, value = ev, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

title: Interactive network graphs in R with canvasXpress
text:
The plot
Pass the two tables as nodeData and edgeData; colorNodeBy colours by the community, and networkLayoutType = "forceDirected" runs the physics simulation.

canvasXpress(
  nodeData          = nodes,
  edgeData          = edges,
  graphType         = "Network",
  networkLayoutType = "forceDirected",
  colorNodeBy       = "group",
  nodeSize          = 25,
  showAnimation     = TRUE,
  title             = "A small community network",
  width             = 650,
  height            = 500
)





Drag any node and the layout settles around it; hover to read the label. The three communities separate on their own because within-group edges outnumber the cross-group ones.

Why “reproducible”
The nodes, edges and config are the figure — one portable specification. The same spec renders the identical network from Python or JavaScript, and can be validated and re-rendered later.

title: Choropleth maps in R with canvasXpress
text: A choropleth shades each region by a value — emissions, incidence, turnout, income. It is the most common map in data analysis and the easiest to get subtly wrong: most “my map is all one colour” complaints are not rendering bugs but scale bugs. This post builds a choropleth in R with canvasXpress that stays vivid and honest on exactly the kind of heavy-tailed data that flattens naive maps. The join and the colouring happen inside the render, so every figure is one portable spec you can re-run from R, Python or the browser.

title: Choropleth maps in R with canvasXpress
section: First, the trap: colour encodes a rate, not a count
text:
First, the trap: colour encodes a rate, not a count
A choropleth fills an area, and area is a size channel your eye cannot help reading. Shade countries by a raw count — total cases, total emissions, total sales — and big, populous regions light up simply because they are big and populous. You have drawn a population map with extra steps.
The fix is almost always to map a rate or density: cases per 100k, emissions per capita, sales per store. Reserve raw counts for a proportional-symbol map (a sized bubble at each centroid), where the size channel carries the count honestly. Decide which question you are answering before you pick the geometry — this one choice prevents most misleading maps.

title: Choropleth maps in R with canvasXpress
text:
One value per region
A choropleth needs exactly one measurement per shape. In canvasXpress the columns are the regions (they match the map by name) and the row is the variable you colour by — here CO₂ emissions per country for 2018. Load a prepared table; swap it for your own (any country → value table works).

library(canvasXpress)

y <- read.table(
  "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-dat.txt",
  header = TRUE, sep = "\t", quote = "", row.names = 1,
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

dim(y)              # 1 row (CO2) x N countries

[1]   1 198

y[, 1:4]

    Afghanistan  Albania  Algeria Andorra
CO2    10.45267 5.402999 164.3093 0.46421


The single row is the variable (CO2); each column name is a country that must match a shape in the map. An optional sample annotation table (rows = countries) rides along for richer tooltips and legends — here the continent and ISO code.

x <- read.table(
  "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-smp.txt",
  header = TRUE, sep = "\t", quote = "", row.names = 1,
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
head(x)

            Code     Continent     Country
Afghanistan  AFG          Asia Afghanistan
Albania      ALB        Europe     Albania
Algeria      DZA        Africa     Algeria
Andorra      AND        Europe     Andorra
Angola       AGO        Africa      Angola
Anguilla     AIA North America    Anguilla

title: Choropleth maps in R with canvasXpress
section: The map: quantile classes computed in R, painted by the map
text:
The map: quantile classes computed in R, painted by the map
graphType = "Map" with a topoJSON of world boundaries draws the shapes and joins the countries by name — no manual merge, no projection math. The statistics stay in R, where they belong: we cut the values into seven quantile classes with quantile() + cut(), so each class holds an equal number of countries (~28 of 198), then colour by that classed annotation with a viridis palette. On skewed data that equal-count guarantee is what keeps all seven colours on the map.

vals   <- as.numeric(y[1, ])
breaks <- unique(quantile(vals, probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 8)))
cls    <- cut(vals, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)
x$Emissions <- sprintf(
  "Q%d: %s", as.integer(cls),
  gsub(",", " - ", gsub("[][()]", "", levels(cls)))[as.integer(cls)]
)
table(x$Emissions)   # ~28 countries per class


Q1: 0.00765 - 0.564    Q2: 0.564 - 2.69      Q3: 2.69 - 7.8      Q4: 7.8 - 22.4 
                 29                  28                  28                  28 
      Q5: 22.4 - 46        Q6: 46 - 208  Q7: 208 - 9.96e+03 
                 28                  28                  29 



canvasXpress(
  data      = y,
  smpAnnot  = x,
  graphType = "Map",
  colorBy   = "Emissions",
  topoJSON  = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
  mapId     = "co2Quantile",
  colors = list("#440154", "#443983", "#31688e", "#21918c",
                "#35b779", "#90d743", "#fde725", "#d9dde3"),
  mapColor        = "#d9dde3",
  mapOutlineColor = "#ffffff",
  legendPosition  = "bottom",
  legendColumns   = 4,
  title    = "CO2 emissions per country (2018)",
  subtitle = "Seven quantile classes computed in R: each colour holds about 28 of 198 countries",
  width  = 760,
  height = 560
)





Every band of the ramp is doing work: the darkest purples are the smallest emitters, the yellows the largest, and the legend states each class’s actual value range — the edges are data-driven, not evenly spaced. The eighth colour, a neutral grey, catches map regions with no data so missing reads as missing. Hover any country for its name, continent, class and value.
If you prefer to keep the classing inside the engine, current CanvasXpress builds accept colorSpectrum (the ramp) plus colorSpectrumBreaksMethod = "quantile" and do the same cut at render time — the R route above works everywhere and keeps the breaks inspectable in your session.

title: Choropleth maps in R with canvasXpress
section: Why not just a plain linear ramp?
text:
Why not just a plain linear ramp?
Because the data is heavy-tailed — a few countries emit thousands of megatonnes while most emit almost nothing. On a linear scale, 195 of these 198 countries fall into the bottom fifth of the range, so a continuous ramp paints nearly the whole world one pale tone and spends its colour on two or three outliers:

canvasXpress(
  data      = y,
  smpAnnot  = x,
  graphType = "Map",
  colorBy   = "CO2",
  topoJSON  = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
  mapId     = "co2Linear",
  legendPosition = "left",
  theme = "solarized",
  title    = "The same data on a plain linear ramp",
  subtitle = "195 of 198 countries sit in the bottom fifth of the scale - the map goes flat",
  width  = 700,
  height = 480
)





This is the single most common choropleth failure. The cure is classing:

colorSpectrumBreaksMethod = "quantile" — equal counts per class. Every colour is used, by construction. The right default for skewed data and for “which regions rank high/low” questions.
colorSpectrumBreaksMethod = "jenks" — natural breaks that minimise within-class variance. Best when the data has genuine clusters with gaps between them; on smoothly heavy-tailed data like this it piles almost everything into the bottom class, so check the legend before you trust it.
Three to seven classes is the usable range — beyond that, readers cannot match colours to the legend.

title: Choropleth maps in R with canvasXpress
text:
Choose the palette on purpose
The palette is not decoration — it is the scale’s grammar:

Sequential (dark → light of ordered hues, like viridis above) for a quantity that only goes up: counts, rates, concentrations.
Diverging (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint) when values are meaningful above and below a reference: change vs. last year, difference from a target, a signed index. Give canvasXpress a three-colour colorSpectrum and pin the midpoint with colorSpectrumZeroValue:
colorBy = "Change",
colorSpectrum = list("#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"),  # blue - neutral - red
colorSpectrumZeroValue = 0                               # value mapped to the middle colour
Never use a diverging palette for a purely positive quantity — the neutral midpoint invents a “normal” that the data does not have.

Viridis and the ColorBrewer ramps are colour-blind-safe and perceptually ordered; a rainbow ramp is neither, so readers cannot tell which end means “more”. Keep the same scale across small multiples so maps stay comparable.

title: Choropleth maps in R with canvasXpress
section: Polish: legend, labels and base styling
text:
Polish: legend, labels and base styling

subtitle / source — caption the units and provenance.
legendNumberFormat = list(style = "decimal", decimals = 1, suffix = "%") — format the legend ticks as percentages, currency, etc.
mapColor / mapOutlineColor — the fill for regions with no data (a neutral grey) and the border between shapes, so missing data reads as missing rather than as a value.
showMapLabels = TRUE — draw region names (best on maps with few regions, e.g. a single country’s provinces; it clutters a 190-country world map).
legendInside = TRUE — float the legend over empty ocean to reclaim width.

title: Choropleth maps in R with canvasXpress
text:
Beyond the world map

Other boundaries. Point topoJSON at any shape file — US states, a single country’s regions, counties, custom districts. The join key is just the shape name.
Projection. mapProjection = "albers" (equal-area, good for the US) or "mercator". Equal-area projections matter for choropleths: Mercator inflates high latitudes, exaggerating those regions’ visual weight.
Categorical maps. Point colorBy at a categorical column (an election winner, a priority tier) for a qualitative choropleth with a discrete legend.
Markers. Add decorations to drop labelled points on cities or call out specific regions.

The whole figure — data, boundaries, classing rule and palette — travels together as one spec, so a reviewer can reproduce it exactly and a colleague can re-render it from Python or JavaScript.

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
text: If you already build plots with ggplot2 or ggpubr, you don’t need to learn a new plotting API to make them interactive. canvasXpress accepts a ggplot object directly: pass it to canvasXpress() and it renders an interactive, reproducible version of the same figure — you keep your existing code.

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
text:
Install

install.packages(c("canvasXpress", "ggpubr"))

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
section: Wrap a plot you already have
text:
Wrap a plot you already have
Here’s an ordinary ggpubr boxplot with pairwise comparisons (geom_pwc) — the significance brackets that show a test between each pair of groups. Build it exactly as you normally would:

library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)

g <- ggboxplot(iris, x = "Species", y = "Sepal.Width", fill = "Species") +
  geom_pwc(method = "t_test", label = "p.format")

Now make it interactive — one call, the same object:

library(canvasXpress)

canvasXpress(g)





That’s the whole idea: no re-specification. canvasXpress reads the ggplot object — its data, aesthetics, layers, scales and the geom_pwc brackets — and renders it. Hover the points, drag to zoom, or open the toolbar to filter and re-style, and the result serializes to one portable spec you can store and reproduce from R, Python or JavaScript.

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
text:
What transfers

Geoms and layers — points, boxes, lines, and stats like geom_pwc / stat_compare_means.
Aesthetic mappings — x, y, fill, color, grouping.
Scales, labels and facets from the ggplot object.

title: Use your ggplot2 (and ggpubr) plots directly with canvasXpress
section: When to reach for the native API instead
text:
When to reach for the native API instead
Wrapping a ggplot is ideal for reusing plots you already have. When you’re building a figure fresh — or want fine control over CanvasXpress-specific features (clustering, dendrograms, interactive annotations) — call canvasXpress() on your data directly with a graphType. See the other posts for that style.

title: Clustered heatmaps in R with canvasXpress
text: The clustered heatmap is the default way to look at an expression matrix: rows and columns reordered by similarity, dendrograms on the margins, and sample metadata alongside. In this post we build one in R with canvasXpress — clustering happens inside the render, so you pass a plain matrix and get an interactive, reproducible figure.

title: Clustered heatmaps in R with canvasXpress
section: An expression matrix with sample metadata
text:
An expression matrix with sample metadata
Swap this simulated block for your own matrix (genes in rows, samples in columns) and a table of per-sample annotations — the output of any normalization/DE pipeline works.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
ng    <- 40                       # genes (rows)
ns    <- 30                       # samples (columns)
genes <- paste0("Gene", seq_len(ng))
samps <- paste0("S", seq_len(ns))
cond  <- rep(c("Tumor", "Normal"), each = ns / 2)

# Two gene blocks, up in one condition each
m <- matrix(rnorm(ng * ns), ng, ns, dimnames = list(genes, samps))
m[ 1:20, cond == "Tumor"]  <- m[ 1:20, cond == "Tumor"]  + 2
m[21:40, cond == "Normal"] <- m[21:40, cond == "Normal"] + 2

canvasXpress takes the matrix as data and a sample annotation table (rows = samples) that becomes an annotation track over the columns.

smpAnnot <- data.frame(Condition = cond, row.names = samps, check.names = FALSE)

title: Clustered heatmaps in R with canvasXpress
text:
The plot
samplesClustered and variablesClustered turn on hierarchical clustering (with dendrograms) on columns and rows; colorSpectrum sets the diverging palette.

canvasXpress(
  data     = as.data.frame(m),
  smpAnnot = smpAnnot,
  graphType = "Heatmap",
  samplesClustered  = TRUE,
  variablesClustered = TRUE,
  colorSpectrum = list("navy", "white", "firebrick3"),
  showSmpDendrogram = TRUE,
  showVarDendrogram = TRUE,
  title = "Clustered expression heatmap",
  width  = 650,
  height = 550
)





The rows and columns are reordered by similarity, the dendrograms show the clustering, and the samples separate cleanly by condition. Hover a cell for its gene, sample and value; the whole figure is one portable spec you can store, validate and re-render.

title: Clustered heatmaps in R with canvasXpress
text:
Scaling up
The same call handles much larger matrices — hundreds of genes by dozens to hundreds of samples — clustering and rendering the full matrix interactively in the browser, not a static image. Point size and labels adapt automatically.

title: Sankey / alluvial diagrams in R with canvasXpress
text: A Sankey (or alluvial) diagram shows how a quantity flows through a sequence of categorical stages — patients moving from a cohort, to a treatment, to an outcome; or reads from a sample, to a mapping status, to a feature. The width of each stream is the magnitude. Here we build one in R with canvasXpress — interactive, and reproducible because the whole figure is one portable spec.

title: Sankey / alluvial diagrams in R with canvasXpress
text:
The data shape
canvasXpress builds a Sankey from a tidy table where each row is one path through the stages, plus a frequency/weight. Swap this simulated clinical flow for your own counts.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
cohort <- c(); treat <- c(); outcome <- c(); freq <- c()
for (co in c("Cohort A", "Cohort B"))
 for (tr in c("Drug 1", "Drug 2", "Placebo"))
  for (ou in c("Response", "Stable", "Progression")) {
    base <- if (ou == "Response") 40 else if (ou == "Stable") 25 else 15
    if (tr == "Placebo" && ou == "Response") base <- 12          # placebo responds less
    cohort  <- c(cohort, co); treat <- c(treat, tr); outcome <- c(outcome, ou)
    freq    <- c(freq, base + sample(0:15, 1))
  }

The value (Freq) is the single measured variable; the stage columns are sample annotations. In canvasXpress terms: one variable × N path-rows, with the categorical stages as smpAnnot.

ids <- paste0("r", seq_along(freq))
y <- data.frame(matrix(freq, nrow = 1, dimnames = list("Freq", ids)), check.names = FALSE)
smpAnnot <- data.frame(Cohort = cohort, Treatment = treat, Outcome = outcome,
                       row.names = ids, check.names = FALSE)

title: Sankey / alluvial diagrams in R with canvasXpress
text:
The plot
graphType = "Sankey" with sankeyAxes listing the stages in order, xAxis naming the value, and colorBy coloring the streams.

canvasXpress(
  data     = y,
  smpAnnot = smpAnnot,
  graphType = "Sankey",
  sankeyAxes = list("Cohort", "Treatment", "Outcome"),
  xAxis      = list("Freq"),
  colorBy    = "Outcome",
  sankeyType = "proportional",
  graphOrientation = "horizontal",
  title = "Patient flow: cohort → treatment → outcome",
  width  = 700,
  height = 500
)





Hover any stream to see the count; the widths are proportional to the frequency, so you can read the flow at a glance — e.g. how much of each cohort ends in Response vs Progression, and how Placebo differs. sankeyType can also be "aligned" (classic alluvial) or "equal".

title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
text: When the same subjects are measured twice — before/after a treatment, baseline vs follow-up — a paired boxplot with a line connecting each subject across the two timepoints tells the story a plain boxplot can’t. This post builds one in R by wrapping a ggpubr ggpaired plot with canvasXpress, so it becomes interactive and reproducible without re-specifying anything.

title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
text:
Install

install.packages(c("canvasXpress", "ggpubr"))

title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
text:
A paired dataset
Long format, two rows per subject — one per timepoint. Swap in your own repeated-measures table.

library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)

set.seed(7)
n  <- 25
df <- data.frame(
  id    = rep(paste0("P", seq_len(n)), 2),
  time  = rep(c("Baseline", "Week 12"), each = n),
  value = c(rnorm(n, 8, 1.2),                       # baseline
            rnorm(n, 8, 1.2) + rnorm(n, -1.2, 0.8)) # follow-up (a drop)
)

title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
section: Build it with ggpaired, then wrap it
text:
Build it with ggpaired, then wrap it
ggpaired draws the two boxes and the per-subject connecting lines; stat_compare_means adds a paired test. Then hand the whole thing to canvasXpress():

library(canvasXpress)

g <- ggpaired(
  df, x = "time", y = "value", id = "id",
  color = "time", line.color = "gray", line.size = 0.3
) +
  stat_compare_means(paired = TRUE, method = "t.test")

canvasXpress(g)





Each grey line is one subject moving from Baseline to Week 12, the boxes summarize each timepoint, and the paired t-test labels the comparison. It’s interactive — hover a line to follow a subject — and the figure is one portable spec you can reproduce from R, Python or JavaScript.

title: Paired before/after boxplots in R with canvasXpress
section: Why paired, not two independent boxes
text:
Why paired, not two independent boxes
A side-by-side boxplot hides who changed. The connecting lines make within-subject change visible: a treatment can lower the group median while a handful of subjects still rise — exactly the pattern you want to catch before drawing conclusions.
